title: Gandhi's Salt March
text:
By early 1930 the Indian National Congress had declared the goal of full independence from Britain, and Gandhi was asked to lead a new campaign of civil disobedience. Colleagues expected a dramatic target. Gandhi chose salt.

British law gave the government a monopoly on making and selling salt and taxed it. Many in Congress thought the issue too small. But salt was needed by everyone, rich and poor, Hindu and Muslim, in every region, and making it from seawater was something anyone could do. Breaking the law would be simple, visible and hard to portray as violent.

On 12 March 1930 Gandhi set out from his ashram at Sabarmati, near Ahmedabad, with 78 followers. He walked about 240 miles to the coastal village of Dandi, speaking in villages along the way, as crowds and the world press followed. On 6 April he picked up a lump of natural salt from the shore, symbolically breaking the law.

Across India, people began making and selling salt illegally. Tens of thousands were arrested, Gandhi among them in May. At the Dharasana salt works, unarmed volunteers marched in rows to be beaten by police without resisting, and the American reporter Webb Miller's account reached readers around the world. In 1931 the viceroy, Lord Irwin, negotiated directly with Gandhi, and the British government invited him to a conference in London.
lesson: Pick a cause that everyone shares and an action that anyone can take. A simple, concrete symbol can unite more people than an abstract demand.
people: Mohandas Gandhi, Lord Irwin, Webb Miller
source: Contemporary press reports; Gandhi's letter to Lord Irwin (2 March 1930); Judith Brown, Gandhi: Prisoner of Hope (1989)
